events.title: Economists confirm a recession
events.description: Researchers identify December 2007 as the end of the expansion. The downturn had begun before your September 2008 decision.

events.title: The Fed lowers rates close to zero
events.description: The Federal Reserve sets its short-term target at 0–0.25% as the economy weakens and borrowing remains difficult.

events.title: Economists date the recession’s end
events.description: Researchers identify June 2009 as the low point. Recovery beginning does not mean conditions have already returned to normal.

events.title: Apple plans to resume dividends
events.description: The company announces payments to shareholders and plans to buy back shares. The first dividend follows in August.

events.title: The Fed continues buying financial assets
events.description: It keeps its short-term interest-rate target near zero and continues buying bonds to support the economy.

what_happened_next.text:
By September 2008, banks and other businesses were in serious trouble. A plan to help banks was rejected in a vote, and AIG, a large insurance company, received emergency help.

The Federal Reserve quickly cut interest rates close to zero. A group that tracks the U.S. economy later said the recession began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009. It did not announce the end date until September 2010. By then, many families and businesses were still struggling.

In 2012, Apple said it would start paying a dividend: money a company pays to people who own its shares. By September 2013, interest rates were still very low.

All three company investments ended above their September 2008 starting values. Apple’s gain was much larger than Microsoft’s or Exxon Mobil’s. But getting to the end was hard to predict; the stocks went through years of change.

A positive five-year result does not mean the frightening months in 2008 were easy to ignore or that recovery was certain.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: People read about a rejected plan to help banks, emergency help for AIG, and rising unemployment. They also followed the election, events in Pakistan, science, music, and new technology.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The crisis brought sharp falls and long months of worry. Later, the economy began to recover, but the three companies did not grow in the same way. A five-year result can hide how much an investment changed on the way.
reflection.what_faded_away: The rescue-plan vote and campaign news soon moved on. The crisis did not end after one vote; more decisions and a long recovery followed. New products and music also gave way to later stories.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In September 2008, no one knew how long the crisis would last, when interest rates would rise again, or how Apple, Microsoft, and Exxon Mobil would change. All three investments ended higher after five years, but that did not make the road there obvious.
